# Repeated Measurements Need a Model for Dependence

Measurements from the same donor, animal, batch, family, site, or experimental
unit tend to resemble one another. Treating them as independent can make standard
errors too small and can assign the wrong sample size to a scientific claim.
Random intercepts and random slopes describe two common sources of structured
heterogeneity:

- a **random intercept** lets units have different baseline levels; and
- a **random slope** lets units respond differently to time, dose, treatment, or
  another within-unit predictor.

The word *random* refers to a probability model for variation across a target
population of groups. It does not imply that group labels were randomized, and
it does not turn an observational association into a causal effect.

# From a Population Line to Unit-specific Lines

Let $Y_{ij}$ be measurement $j$ from unit $i$, and let $x_{ij}$ be a predictor
that can vary within a unit. A random-intercept and random-slope model is

$$
\boxed{
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0i}+b_{1i}x_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}.
}
$$

The population-average conditional line is
$\beta_0+\beta_1x$. Unit $i$ has line

$$
(\beta_0+b_{0i})+(\beta_1+b_{1i})x.
$$

Here $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are **fixed-effect parameters**: shared
population-level coefficients to be estimated. The latent deviations $b_{0i}$
and $b_{1i}$ are **random effects**. A standard Gaussian specification is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0i}\\b_{1i}\end{pmatrix}
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
N\!\left[
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \tau_{01}\\
\tau_{01} & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right],
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2),
$$

with random effects independent of residual errors under the model. The
parameters have distinct meanings:

| Quantity | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| $\beta_0$ | mean outcome at $x=0$ in the target population |
| $\beta_1$ | mean change in outcome per unit change in $x$ |
| $\tau_0^2$ | between-unit variance in intercepts |
| $\tau_1^2$ | between-unit variance in slopes |
| $\tau_{01}$ | intercept--slope covariance |
| $\sigma^2$ | within-unit residual variance after modeled effects |

An estimand might be the population mean slope $\beta_1$, the between-donor
slope variance $\tau_1^2$, or a prediction for a future donor. The fitting
procedure defines an **estimator** of that target; a fitted numerical value is
the **estimate**. These goals require different uncertainty summaries.

# Random Intercepts Induce Within-unit Correlation

Set $b_{1i}=0$ temporarily. Conditional on $b_{0i}$, repeated outcomes are
independent with mean $\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0i}$. After integrating over the
unobserved intercept,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid\mathbf x_i)=\tau_0^2+\sigma^2
$$

and, for $j\ne k$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}\mid\mathbf x_i)=\tau_0^2.
$$

The resulting intraclass correlation coefficient is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{ICC}=\frac{\tau_0^2}{\tau_0^2+\sigma^2}.
}
$$

It is the model-implied correlation of two residualized measurements from the
same unit. It is not the fraction of observations that are duplicates, nor does
it have a single context-free value when slopes, heteroskedasticity, or further
levels are present.

# Random Slopes Make Covariance Depend on the Predictor

With both random effects, the covariance of two measurements from unit $i$ is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}\mid\mathbf x_i)
=\tau_0^2+(x_{ij}+x_{ik})\tau_{01}
+x_{ij}x_{ik}\tau_1^2+\mathbb{1}(j=k)\sigma^2.
}
$$

Thus a random-slope model is not merely a device for drawing different lines.
It specifies a covariance pattern that changes with the measurement locations.
Two late time points can be more strongly correlated than an early and a late
time point because both depend heavily on $b_{1i}$.

The correlation

$$
\rho_{01}=\frac{\tau_{01}}{\tau_0\tau_1}
$$

describes whether units above the mean at $x=0$ tend to change faster or more
slowly. Its interpretation depends on where zero is placed. Replacing $x$ by
$x-c$ changes the intercept and its covariance with the slope even though the
fitted trajectories are unchanged. Center time or dose at a scientifically
meaningful reference and state that reference explicitly.

# Within-unit and Between-unit Effects Can Differ

If $x_{ij}$ varies within units, one coefficient for $x_{ij}$ can conflate two
questions. Write

$$
x_{ij}=\bar x_i+(x_{ij}-\bar x_i)
$$

and model

$$
Y_{ij}=\beta_0
+\beta_{\mathrm{between}}\bar x_i
+\beta_{\mathrm{within}}(x_{ij}-\bar x_i)
+b_{0i}+b_{1i}(x_{ij}-\bar x_i)+\varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

$\beta_{\mathrm{within}}$ compares two measurements from the same unit at
different predictor values; $\beta_{\mathrm{between}}$ compares units with
different average predictor values. They need not be equal. Group-mean
centering makes this distinction explicit, but it does not remove time-varying
confounding or measurement error.

# Partial Pooling and Unit-specific Prediction

Estimating every unit separately is noisy when each unit has few measurements.
Forcing every unit to share one line ignores heterogeneity. Mixed models
partially pool: unit-specific effects are pulled toward the population line by an
amount determined by their precision and the estimated variance components.

In matrix form for one unit,

$$
\mathbf y_i=\mathbf X_i\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf Z_i\mathbf b_i+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i,
$$

the empirical best linear unbiased predictor is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf b}_i
=\widehat{\mathbf G}\mathbf Z_i^\mathsf{T}
\widehat{\mathbf V}_i^{-1}
(\mathbf y_i-\mathbf X_i\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}),
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf V}_i
=\mathbf Z_i\widehat{\mathbf G}\mathbf Z_i^\mathsf{T}
+\widehat{\mathbf R}_i.
$$

Units with sparse or noisy observations receive stronger shrinkage. These
predictions are often called BLUPs or conditional modes. They are not raw group
means and should not be treated as error-free observed covariates in a second
analysis. Ranking units without prediction intervals can badly overstate
differences, especially for small groups.

# Choosing a Random-effects Structure from the Design

The random-effects structure should represent how the experiment generated
replicated comparisons.

- Include a random intercept when repeated observations share a unit-level
  baseline source of variation.
- Consider a random slope when a predictor varies within units and the target
  population plausibly contains heterogeneous responses.
- A random slope is weakly identified when most units have only one predictor
  value, too few occasions, or nearly identical occasions.
- Crossed factors require separate terms when, for example, every specimen is
  measured by several operators and every operator measures several specimens.
- Nested terms are appropriate when lower-level labels occur within exactly one
  higher-level unit, such as wells within plates.

Adding every conceivable covariance parameter can exceed the information in the
design. Conversely, omitting design-supported slope variation can make
fixed-effect tests anticonservative. A defensible structure is prespecified from
the sampling and randomization scheme, checked for estimability, and subjected
to sensitivity analysis rather than chosen solely by the smallest p-value.

# Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Sensitivity

| Assumption or issue | Diagnostic question | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Correct mean structure | Do conditional residuals show curvature, time trends, or interactions? | revise the mean model using scientifically justified terms |
| Adequate random-effects structure | Does heterogeneity remain by unit, time, or treatment? | compare design-supported intercept/slope structures |
| Gaussian random effects | Are conclusions driven by a few extreme unit predictions? | inspect prediction distributions and refit with robust or alternative models |
| Residual variance model | Does spread change with time, group, or fitted value? | model heterogeneous variance or use an appropriate outcome model |
| Independence across units | Are units related by batch, family, site, or donor? | represent the additional level or dependence source |
| Random effects independent of modeled predictors | Could latent baseline differences also determine exposure? | add measured unit-level causes or use a design/causal model that addresses endogeneity |
| Sufficient support | Are variance estimates near zero or correlations near $\pm1$? | simplify only with design and sensitivity evidence; report boundary behavior |

A **singular fit** places the estimated covariance matrix on or near its
boundary, for example with $\widehat\tau_1^2=0$ or
$|\widehat\rho_{01}|=1$. It may indicate that the data cannot support the
specified structure, but it is not automatically proof that the true variance
is zero. Check coding, scaling, group counts, predictor spread within groups,
optimizer diagnostics, and whether the design identifies the component.

Variance-component tests are nonregular because zero lies on the boundary of
the parameter space. Routine chi-squared reference distributions can be wrong.
Use a method justified for the boundary problem, such as a carefully specified
parametric bootstrap, and emphasize interval estimates and scientific
sensitivity rather than a binary keep/drop decision.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Suppose gene expression is measured at baseline, 6 hours, and 24 hours for cells
derived from 40 donors under control and stimulation. Several wells and
sequencing libraries are prepared per donor--condition combination.

For a claim about human response heterogeneity, the donor is the experimental
unit. Wells, libraries, and reads are technical levels unless the target
population explicitly concerns those processes. A model might include a donor
random intercept, a donor random slope for stimulation or time, fixed effects
for condition, time, and their interaction, and batch terms supported by the
design. The condition-by-time coefficient estimates the mean response pattern;
the random-slope variance estimates heterogeneity around that mean.

Statistically, evidence of nonzero slope variation means that donor trajectories
are more dispersed than a common-slope model allows under the specified
distribution. Biologically, it does not by itself reveal the molecular cause of
heterogeneity. Donor covariates, cell composition, measurement error, and batch
structure remain competing explanations. Forty donors—not the number of cells,
wells, libraries, or reads—primarily determine information about population
heterogeneity.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Multiple linear regression](../regression-models/multiple-linear-regression.qmd)
  supplies the fixed conditional-mean component.
- [Linear-model assumptions and diagnostics](../regression-models/linear-model-assumptions-and-diagnostics.qmd)
  explains residual, leverage, and mean-structure checks.
- [Shrinkage estimation](shrinkage-estimation.qmd) develops partial pooling as a
  bias--variance trade-off.
- [Empirical Bayes](empirical-bayes.qmd) explains plug-in hyperparameter
  estimation and conditional prediction.
- [Linear mixed-effects models](linear-mixed-effects-models.qmd) develops the
  general matrix model, estimation, fixed-effect inference, and prediction.
- [Confidence intervals](../statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd) and
  [parametric bootstrap](../statistical-inference/parametric-bootstrap.qmd)
  provide uncertainty tools used with mixed models.

1. Random intercepts model baseline heterogeneity and induce within-unit
   correlation; random slopes model heterogeneous change and predictor-dependent
   covariance.
2. Centering controls the meaning of the intercept and intercept--slope
   covariance; separating within- and between-unit predictors prevents an
   important interpretive conflation.
3. Unit-specific effects are shrunken predictions with uncertainty, not directly
   observed attributes.
4. The sampling, nesting, and randomization design should determine the candidate
   random-effects structure.
5. Technical replication can improve measurement but does not replace biological
   replication for estimating population heterogeneity.
